title: Ari Cascade Peak Pro Review: Affordable and Adaptable – Travis Engel
content:
Designing and speccing a budget full-suspension bike is a puzzle, and every brand solves it differently. They predict where a customer is willing to splurge, and where they want to save. Travis thinks the Ari Cascade Peak strikes an even balance, in more ways than one.

If you’re shopping for a high-end carbon full suspension bike, you’re spoiled for choice these days. Not only between brands, but within brands. Most offer four or five price points in each model. But there’s no such bounty on the alloy end of the spectrum. You’re lucky to get two builds: The cheap one that makes far too many compromises, and the one you should actually buy.

Ari Cascade Peak Pro Quick Hits

  • 135mm rear travel, 140mm front
  • 29” wheels, front and rear
  • Alloy frame only
  • Two in-triangle bottle cages on all sizes
  • 35.9 lbs (XL w/o pedals)
  • Assorted spec customizations available at purchase
  • Assembled in Utah
  • Sold consumer-direct
  • Entry-level build starts at $2,199
  • $3,384 as tested

The Ari Cascade Peak lineup is different. This 135mm rear-travel, 140mm front-travel do-it-all trail bike comes in three stock builds: The $2,200 Comp, the $2,800 Elite, and the $3,300 Pro. I usually save spec talk for the end of my reviews, but this one deserves a spotlight. I’d never been so torn on which price point to cover.

I leaned towards the Comp at first. It’s impressive to get in under $3K in 2026. Its DVO suspension has a boutique cache, with bonus versatility points for the fork’s 36mm stanchions. And it runs on the proven Deore 6100 drivetrain with a proper 10-51 12-speed Micro Spline cassette. But then the base-level Comp grabbed me. Its MicroShift AdventX drivetrain has a populist appeal, and its Shimano two-piston brakes are better than Tektro. Though  when speccing suspension, I think it was brave for Ari to go off-brand. At lower pricepoints, a Suntour fork and shock are often better than similarly priced RockShox stuff.

But I ultimately chose the Pro build. Deore 7200 may become the benchmark for affordable high-end hanger-mount cable-actuated drivetrains. And Ari swapped in an XT 8200 shifter for its double-upshift capability. The Reynolds alloy rims will save some unsprung rotational weight, and the recently updated TRP EVO Expert brake is remarkably powerful. The Marzocchi suspension is the Cascade Peak Pro’s most meaningful upgrade. Marzocchi is now the Fox budget label, with similar functionality, a little less adjustability, and a little more weight. There’s lots to say about it, but I’ll save that for the ride impressions.

Customization and Ordering

Ari assembles their bikes in their Utah headquarters. That makes for improved quality control, wider inventory flexibility, and a few more American jobs. It also allows for customizations and substitutions. Far more than other locally assembled brands like Pivot and Yeti offer. The Cascade Peak’s add-to-cart process includes tweaks like adding a tubeless setup, upgrading your wheels, or applying frame protection. But I got my build with 50mm rise bars and a 230mm dropper post, which were technically off-menu. If you want something that’s not in the drop-downs email Ari and they may be able to accommodate. Just email them. It’s a surprisingly concierge-level process. I even got texts as my review bike went through picking, building, checking, and shipping.

Of course, Ari is only able to offer that experience at these prices because they sell consumer-direct. Given that this review shares server space with The Radavist’s many shop visits and human stories, I need to acknowledge that high-end consumer-direct sales are a disruptive force among US retailers. I try to call that out when I review these bikes, but that doesn’t mean I get to have it both ways. In the grand scheme of things, I believe it’s good that consumer-direct bikes are an option. Especially budget-friendly ones like the Ari Cascade Peak.

Ari Cascade Peak Frame Design

The Cascade Peak is effectively the alloy version of the all-carbon Delano Peak, which has 10 mm more fork travel, and a longer-stroke shock for an extra 7 mm out back. Ari gave these two models unique names so they were free to evolve at different intervals, and potentially even in different directions. Thankfully, the Cascade Peak seems pretty future-proof. Its Horst-style linkage doesn’t really take any chances, nor should it. The pivots are all bearings, and they’re all big. There’s a flip chip (in its default “low” setting) that’s so sleek, I didn’t notice it until I was cleaning the bike ahead of its return. It’s got a threaded bottom bracket, press-in headset cups, ample tire clearance, and a pretty slick paint job.

I do have a few nitpicks. The cables rattled inside the frame, though Ari jiu-jitsu’d that into something praise-worthy. I brought it up in a debrief with Tyler Cloward, Ari’s Director of Product Development. A few days later, he said they took the note and will make a rolling change to foam-line their unguided internal housing at no extra charge.

Fair play, Ari. Now route your shift housing through the top of the chainstay not the bottom. It makes for a smoother line than the Cascade Peak’s under-stay exit, though I know it’s far from the only bike that does it. Another note while we’re back there: The chainstay protection is ample, but my foot began peeling it off on my very first ride. A few zip ties fixed it, but the stays are relatively wide if you know you’re particularly sensitive to heel clicking. And finally, the frame has an oddly tall silhouette. But there’s a very good reason for that.

This is the second bike in a row I’ve tested with two in-triangle bottle cages, and I hope it’s the next big trend in trail bikes. Especially given the hot summer we’ve had here in LA, I’ve been thankful to stay hydrated without the aid of a full-sized hydration pack. It’s a quantitative increase with qualitative impact. I can carry nearly 100 ounces of water by adding a two-bottle hip pack. Or I can just rely on my bib pockets, and still get 44 ounces. One bottle can be for water, the other can be for fancy chemicals. And there’s still a little pocket of space at the front of the triangle to strap on an essentials kit, though I wouldn’t have minded an accessory port. Of course, I could strap my essentials to the under-downtube mount. Or, I could run a third bottle.

Ari Cascade Peak Geometry

Depending on how you measure standover, all that storage comes at a cost of 20 to 30 mm of clearance compared to similar single-bottle bikes. But I think standover is more about form than function. A low top tube makes a mountain bike look like it came to party. And while the Cascade Peak is no pooper, it’s more about broad versatility than pure velocity. Its 65° head angle is conservative by today’s trail-bike standards, as is its wheelbase. The high-ish bottom bracket favors pedaling over plantedness, and the 434mm chainstays (across all sizes) are about as short as they come in this category. And yet, it’s got a burly fork, big rotors, and brakes that have become downhill darlings. If you’re looking for a bike that’ll clearly tell you what it wants, this isn’t it. So, what does it want?

Ari Cascade Peak Ride Impressions: Climbing

I reviewed Ari’s (then Fezz-ari’s) La Sal peak in 2018, and I gushed about its 78° seat-tube angle. It was revolutionary back then, and it’s actually still pretty steep today. It pairs well with the Cascade Peak’s active rear suspension. It’s got a slightly floaty feel that is saved from wallowing by its forward weight bias. But that means it isn’t the kind of mid-travel trail bike that encourages you to mash at race pace. The Pivot Trailcat and Ibis Ripley are much more energetic. The Cascade Peak favors plushness over pep. That means I relied on the lockout lever to optimize long, smooth climbs, which is a fair trade for how this bike performed when things got technical.

There wasn’t that magical hoverbike effect offered by some DW and CBF bikes that provides a stable platform while the rear wheel simultaneously pours effortlessly through obstacles. But the Cascade Peak would yield with impeccable consistency. There was no sudden drop-off or unwelcomed ramp-up in support. That offered a lot of freedom in setups. I tend to want a little deeper sag in my rear suspension, and there were no mushy consequences when I took poor lines or showed poor form. And I had to do both at the same time to get my foot in the dirt. After a month of testing, only one pedal strike was severe enough to remember.

Equally forgiving on the climbs was the Cascade Peak’s wheelbase. To be fair, I’ve spent a number of years riding enduro bikes as daily drivers. Your mileage may vary, but the Cascade Peak should be easy for anyone to get used to. In a word, its climbing vibe is “comfortable.” That suits a bike like this rather well. The ample on-bike storage was ideal for epic rides at steady paces. Meanwhile, its spec and chassis adeptly handled most of the descents I found along the way … but not all of them.

Ari Cascade Peak Ride Impressions: Descending

Bikes in this travel category often suffer from an identity crisis. They’re not as plush as all-mountain bikes, and they’re not as zippy as short-travel trail bikes. A brand can inject some personality with a high pivot and long chainstay like the Forbidden Druid or an extravagant lightweight build like the Pivot Trailcat LT. The Cascade Peak does neither, and yet it still makes some clear choices in its on-trail behavior. Namely; it likes the techy stuff.

Just like on the climbs, it’s quite agreeable to quick maneuvers on awkward terrain. That’s not true of many bikes north of 130mm rear travel. But the consistency I sensed on the climbs returned to help make the Cascade Peak remarkably responsive on the descents. It was easy to pop one or both wheels off the ground to maintain the right line with the right momentum. Paired with the moderate geo, this made for a nimble ride that I wouldn’t have expected from a bike with this much travel and this much mass.

If you like the sound of that, I do recommend opting for taller bars. I mean, I always recommend taller bars, but defaulting to a more upright, mid-bike body position gave me a better starting point when making these maneuvers. It also helped on straighter, faster descents. And the Cascade Peak does need a little help in that department.

I need to first acknowledge that my career in covering high-end mountain bikes has left me a little spoiled. That usually doesn’t get in the way when I’m reviewing affordable bikes like the Cascade Peak. My overall judgement is never clouded by the absence (or presence) of carbon wheels or electronic drivetrains. But suspension is different, especially front suspension. High-end dampers can combine support and sensitivity in ways simpler designs can’t. And the Marzocchi Z1’s Rail damper is indeed a simple design. It’s robust and low-maintenance, but it lacks the speed-sensitive nuances of Fox’s Grip damper or RockShox’s Charger.

On the trail, that meant high-intensity impacts were a little harsh off the top. To my surprise, though, the fork wasn’t diving excessively or getting otherwise overwhelmed. The ride height defaulted up where I wanted it. But at high speeds and on rough terrain, I couldn’t get into the flow a bike like this should be capable of. Again, keep in mind I’m coming off a Fox 36 SL, which itself followed the almost-too-plush RockShox Lyrik Linear XL. Those are extremely high bars. Once I had acclimated to the Z1’s feel, its relatively mild shortcomings became less and less distracting. And to many Cascade Peak customers, it may be the best fork they’ve ever ridden.

The 36mm chassis is a smart long-term choice for a versatile bike that may end up literally anywhere. But as an experiment on my last few rides, I swapped it for a Fox fork equipped with their Grip X damper. It made a significant difference. The whole bike was suddenly able to float more calmly through chunder.

This got me thinking about Ari’s customization. Cloward tells me they technically could accommodate a buyer’s request to upgrade to a higher-end fork. But that would bump the highest-end Cascade Peak Pro up to within a few hundred bucks of the $4,200 entry-level Delano Peak Comp. That bike’s DVO Diamond 36 D1 SL offers speed-sensitive damping tech similar to what makes Fox’s 36 Grip X damper so ubiquitous in the high end. And it’s got a carbon frame. Or there’s the $5,300 Delano Peak Expert, which gets a highly tunable 36 Grip X2 damper, plus upgrades nearly everywhere else.

But let’s take a step back from that slippery slope. If I’ve made you doubt the Cascade Peak’s front suspension performance, but the bike is already at the top of your price range, you can always upgrade the fork damper to a Grip X. You can easily make the swap at home with a chamferless socket bit. And it’s $320, which is about half what it’d cost for Ari to upgrade to a Fox 36. You’ll still have a more basic air spring, but so did the two-generation-old Fox fork I bolted on. And anyway, I said no more slippery slopes. You can make this upgrade at any point down the road. There’s no rush. But if that time comes, the bike deserves it.

The rest of the build lives up to the bike’s potential. That Deore 7200 drivetrain shifts great and is surprisingly quiet despite its clutch-less-ness. It seemed somehow calmer than my XTR Di2 drivetrain. Maybe because it gets support from a length of stiff SIS housing, and because it lacks the weight of a motor and battery. The recently updated TRP brakes are just as impressive. The sharp bend at the blade tip is a bit love-or-hate, but the power is all love. They feel a lot like Hayes Dominion A4, if you’ve ever been fortunate enough to try those.

The TranzX dropper post is fast and firm, the Continental Xynotal / Kryptotal tires are overkill in the best way, and … well, look at that. I am ending on spec. I guess it’s an important factor here. If we were talking about a $6,500 mountain bike, we could rightly assume it would offer total functional perfection. It’s not so simple at half the price, but the Cascade Peak Pro manages with very few compromises.

All that’s left is to explain what kind of mountain bike it is. To outline its likes and dislikes. Again, the Cascade Peak likes little techy sections and big long pedals. But it’s well enough equipped that it has very few dislikes. That’s how it should be in this broadly appealing category at this broadly appealing price point. It’ll handle just about any trail you put in front of it without ever leaving you wishing it was anything other than exactly what it is.

Pros:

  • Surprisingly nimble for a mid-travel trail bike
  • Comfortable climbing position
  • Two in-triangle bottle cages!
  • Worth upgrading down the road
  • Good value
  • Smart spec
  • Wide customization options

Cons:

  • Fork is a bit harsh at high speeds
  • Geometry isn’t as DH-ready as that of some bikes in this travel category
